# Terminal Deck

> Terminal Deck is a free, MIT-licensed desktop application for macOS that runs AI coding-agent sessions — Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI — in a single window. Each session gets a tab with a live status dot classified from what is drawn on that session's terminal screen, and cost, token use and context-window pressure are read from Claude Code's own JSONL transcripts. It is at version 0.1.0 and runs from source; there is no packaged installer yet. It has no account, no telemetry and no analytics.

This file is every page of https://terminaldeck.dev as one markdown document.
Version 0.1.0. Built by Asad Iqbal. MIT licensed.
Repository: https://github.com/asadev/terminaldeck

---

# Home

Source: https://terminaldeck.dev/

## Run your coding agents on one deck

Terminal Deck is a macOS desktop app for Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI.
Run several sessions side by side, see at a glance which ones are working and
which are waiting on you, and know what they cost.

**Where this is up to.** Version 0.1.0. It runs on macOS from source — there is
no packaged installer, no auto-update and no signed build yet.

## What Terminal Deck is

Terminal Deck is a free, MIT-licensed desktop application for macOS that runs AI
coding-agent sessions — Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI — in a single
window. Each session gets a tab with a live status dot classified from what is
actually drawn on that session's terminal screen, so working, waiting and
needs-input never look the same. Cost, token use and context-window pressure are
read from Claude Code's own JSONL transcripts rather than scraped from terminal
output. Alongside the terminals it carries a chat view of a session's
conversation with a composer, an embedded browser whose element inspector turns a
clicked element into a CSS selector for the agent, a git panel, a file tree,
full-text search across past transcripts, a GitHub panel, an MCP inspector, hook
management, AI-readiness scoring, isolated agent profiles, a swarm view and a
settings window. It is built by Asad Iqbal. At version 0.1.0 it is run from
source; there is no packaged download yet. Nothing it does leaves the machine —
there is no account, no telemetry and no analytics.

## Why

Running agents in bare terminal tabs falls apart quickly. You lose track of which
session is mid-thought and which has been sitting on a question for ten minutes,
you have no idea what you have spent, and there is nothing between an agent and
your files when it decides to do something drastic.

## What works today

- **Sessions in tabs.** Several sessions per project, each with its own terminal.
  Scrollback survives switching away and coming back.
- **Status at a glance.** Every tab carries a dot: working, waiting, needs input
  or exited. It is classified in the main process, so background tabs stay
  accurate.
- **Chat view.** The same session, read as a conversation — prompts and replies,
  none of the tool plumbing. The composer types into the session, so the terminal
  agrees.
- **Cost and context.** Spend per session, project and day, read from Claude
  Code's transcripts. Cache reads and the two cache-write rates are priced
  separately.
- **Session inspector.** `⌘⇧I` opens a timeline, a cost breakdown, tool-usage
  stats and a context meter for the focused session.
- **Embedded browser.** Load a page in a tab, click an element, and its CSS
  selector and text go to the agent as context. Guest pages stay isolated from
  the app.
- **Project workspace.** Git panel, file tree and viewer, quick open, a command
  palette, and a GitHub panel driven by the `gh` CLI.
- **Agent profiles.** Separate logins side by side. Each profile gets its own
  `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so work and personal accounts never mix.
- **Swarm and splits.** `⌘\` shows every running session in one grid. Panes split
  right and down with focus routing.

## What the status dots mean

Agent CLIs are full-screen programs that repaint by moving the cursor, so the
tail of the output stream tells you nothing about the bottom of the screen. Each
session therefore feeds a background terminal emulator, and the status is read
from that emulator's viewport — what a human would see.

- Working — the agent is thinking or running a tool
- Waiting — the prompt is back, nothing is running
- Needs input — a question is on screen and blocking
- Exited — the process is gone

## One decision worth knowing

Sessions run with the login shell's `PATH`. A GUI app on macOS inherits a minimal
environment and genuinely cannot see `claude`, so the path is resolved once by
asking the login shell, and every session inherits it. This is the difference
between the app working and the app insisting you have not installed anything.

## Requirements

- macOS. Linux and Windows are not yet exercised.
- Node 22 or newer.
- At least one agent CLI installed and authenticated — Claude Code, Codex CLI or
  Gemini CLI. A plain shell also works if you just want the tabs.

## Running it

```
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Licence

MIT. Free, and free to fork. Built by Asad Iqbal.

# Features

Source: https://terminaldeck.dev/features.html

Everything below is in the app today. What is not built yet has its own section
at the bottom.

## Sessions and status

A project holds as many sessions as you want, each one a real process in its own
terminal. Tabs live in the window header; scrollback is replayed when you switch
back, so leaving a tab does not lose what happened while you were away. Sessions
can be started with Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI or a plain shell, chosen
per session, per project or globally.

Every tab carries a status dot. The classification does not read the output
stream — agent CLIs repaint by moving the cursor, so the tail of the stream has
no relationship to the bottom of the screen. Each session instead feeds a
headless terminal emulator in the main process and the status is read from that
emulator's viewport, which means background tabs are classified as accurately as
the visible one. The four states are working, waiting, needs input and exited.

Around that: unread indicators when output arrives on a background tab, desktop
notifications and sounds when a session finishes or needs you, session titles
derived from the conversation rather than the folder name, and `⌘⇧T` to continue
a project's last conversation.

## Chat mode

The same session, read as a conversation. Chat mode reads Claude Code's own
transcript and shows only what a person said and what the agent said back — tool
calls, usage blocks and compaction markers are thrown away, because hiding them
is the entire point of the view.

The rules for what counts as a typed prompt were measured against the transcripts
on a real machine rather than assumed. A `user` line is only a prompt when its
content is a string; the array form is almost always tool results, and rendering
those turns the agent's own output into fake user messages.

The composer at the bottom writes to the session's terminal exactly as if you had
typed there, because that is where the agent is listening. There is no second
channel to keep in sync, and a message sent from chat appears in the terminal
view too.

## Cost and context

Claude Code writes JSONL transcripts under `~/.claude/projects/`. That is the
source for all of this — nothing is scraped from terminal output. A watcher tails
the file per session and the numbers follow: spend per session, per project and
per day, token counts, and how full the context window is with a warning when it
bloats.

Cache traffic is priced properly. A cache read is a tenth of the input rate, a
five-minute cache write is 1.25×, and a one-hour write — which is what Claude
Code actually writes — is 2×. Charging every write at the five-minute rate
under-reports a long session's spend by 37.5% on the cached portion.

## Inspector, search and alerts

- **Session inspector** (`⌘⇧I`). A timeline of the session, a cost breakdown,
  tool-usage statistics and a context meter.
- **Transcript search.** Full-text search across past transcripts — this project
  or every project — returning ranked results with highlighted snippets.
- **Smart alerts.** Missing tools, context bloat, session health. Built around
  one rule: a brand-new project must be silent.

## The project workspace

- **Git panel.** Branch, dirty files and diffs, kept current by a watcher.
- **File tree and viewer.** Browse the project and read files with syntax
  highlighting.
- **Quick open and palette.** `⌘P` for files, `⌘K` for commands, both
  fuzzy-matched.
- **GitHub panel.** Open pull requests, open issues and the unread notification
  count, through the `gh` CLI,
  with unread badges. "Not logged in" and "no GitHub remote" never look the same.
- **AI readiness score.** Does the project have a CLAUDE.md, a README, tests,
  lint, typecheck, a gitignore and a clean git state — with one-click fixes. A
  committed `.env` caps the score below every band.
- **`.deckignore`.** One list of what the app should not look at, honoured by the
  tree, quick open, search and the watchers, with gitignore semantics.

## Dashboard and board

Each project gets a drag-and-drop widget grid — sessions, cost, git, GitHub, AI
readiness and the Kanban board — and a Kanban board of its own with search and
tag filtering. A card can start or resume a session, and moves to Done when that
session completes.

## Many sessions at once

- **Swarm view** (`⌘\`) puts every running session in one grid, sized so each
  cell is still wide enough to read a prompt.
- **Agent profiles.** Each profile gets its own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, which makes
  it a separate login with separate history and transcripts. Set per session, per
  project or globally.

Profile isolation was checked against the real CLI, not assumed. Credentials live
in the macOS Keychain under a service name derived from the config directory, so
a second login cannot overwrite the first one's token — and deleting a profile's
folder does not log it out.

## The embedded browser

A browser tab lives in the same window as the sessions. Load a page, turn on
inspect, click an element, and the app hands the agent a CSS selector, a label
and one line of context.

The guest page is untrusted, so it only reports facts about the clicked element —
tag, id, whether that id is unique, position among its siblings. Every judgement
about which selector wins and what is safe to paste into a terminal happens on
the trusted side, where it is tested against hostile input rather than hoped
about.

The browser also carries a device bar that resizes the real Chromium view rather
than scaling a screenshot, so a 390px phone frame is a 390px viewport and media
queries actually fire; a step recorder that turns what you did into a readable
flow you can send to the agent; per-tab session isolation; and an import of your
existing Chrome configuration.

## Integrations

- **MCP inspector.** Reads your own Claude Code MCP configuration rather than
  keeping a second list, connects to servers, and lists and calls their tools
  from a generated form.
- **Provider hooks.** Hooks installed into each CLI's real settings file, tagged
  `terminaldeck-hook`. Nothing is ever removed for merely looking like ours — a
  machine running another tool keeps its own hooks.
- **Settings window.** Eleven sections: general, appearance, notifications,
  agents, setup, browser, shortcuts, profiles, advanced, help and about. Themes
  apply live, terminals included.

## Not built yet

- P2P session sharing
- Auto-updating from our own releases
- Translations — the app is English only
- Code signing and notarisation. The `.dmg` itself is built; nothing signs it.
- Split panes. The layout code and the `⌘D` / `⌘⇧S` / `⌘⇧W` chords exist in the
  repository, but nothing in the app renders the split view, so it cannot be
  reached.
- A tested Intel build — one is produced by the same command and has never been
  launched — and anything at all on Linux or Windows.

---

# Docs

Source: https://terminaldeck.dev/docs/

Terminal Deck is at version 0.1.0. `npm run dist:mac` packages it into an
unsigned `.dmg` and `.zip` for arm64 and x64; there is no published, signed
installer, so most people run it from source in development mode.

## Requirements

- **macOS.** Linux and Windows are not yet exercised — parts of the app depend on
  macOS behaviour, notably how agent logins are stored.
- **Node 22 or newer.**
- **At least one agent CLI, installed and authenticated.** Claude Code, Codex CLI
  or Gemini CLI. Terminal Deck starts the CLI you already have; it does not ship
  or proxy one, and it never sees your API keys.

A plain shell also works as a session type if you only want the tabs, the status
dots and the workspace panels.

## Running it

```
git clone https://github.com/asadev/terminaldeck.git
cd terminaldeck
npm install
npm run dev
```

`npm run dev` starts Electron with the renderer hot-reloading. Changes to the
main process need a restart; renderer changes do not.

```
npm test          # vitest
npm run typecheck # both tsconfigs
npm run build     # production bundle
```

**Do not run `npm run build` while `npm run dev` is serving.** They share the
`out/` directory, and the build overwrites what dev is running.

## First run

1. Open a project with `⌘O`. Projects are remembered between launches.
2. Start a session with `⌘T`, choosing the agent for this session. The default
   comes from the project, then from your preferences.
3. Watch the tab's dot. Working, waiting, needs input and exited are the four
   states, and they are read from what the session actually draws on screen.
4. Open the settings window with `⌘,`. The Setup section reports which CLIs it
   found.

## Keyboard map

Every binding is in the app's own shortcut sheet, which opens with `⌘/`.

Sessions and projects:

| Action | Keys |
|---|---|
| New session | `⌘T` |
| Resume the last session here | `⌘⇧T` |
| Close session | `⌘W` |
| Jump to a session tab | `⌘1`–`⌘9` |
| Next session | `⌃Tab` |
| Previous session | `⌃⇧Tab` |
| Open a project | `⌘O` |
| Quick open a file | `⌘P` or `⌘⇧O` |
| Command palette | `⌘K` or `⌘⇧P` |

Panels and layout:

| Action | Keys |
|---|---|
| Task board | `⌘⇧B` |
| Project dashboard | `⌘⇧D` |
| File tree | `⌘⇧E` |
| Git panel | `⌘⇧G` |
| Session inspector | `⌘⇧I` |
| Swarm view | `⌘\` |
| Toggle the sidebar | `⌘B` |
| Preferences | `⌘,` |
| Keyboard shortcuts | `⌘/` |

Inside a terminal:

| Action | Keys |
|---|---|
| Find in the terminal | `⌘F` |
| Clear the terminal | `⌘⇧K` |
| Copy the selection | `⌘⇧C` |
| Interrupt the agent (passes through) | `⌃C` |
| Stop what the agent is doing (passes through) | `Esc` |

## Where it keeps things

- **App state** — your projects, preferences and window bounds live in
  `state.json` in the app's user-data directory, written atomically.
- **Transcripts** — Terminal Deck does not write them. It reads the ones Claude
  Code already keeps under `~/.claude/projects/`, and that is where cost,
  context, search and chat mode all come from.
- **Profiles** — each agent profile is a directory that becomes that session's
  `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Credentials stay in the macOS Keychain, not in the
  directory, so deleting a profile folder does not log it out.
- **Hook backups** — before a hook is written into a CLI's settings, the original
  is copied into `~/.terminaldeck/hook-backups/`.

## When it cannot find your agent

The most common problem, and it is not your installation. A GUI app on macOS
inherits a minimal `PATH` — it does not run your shell profile — so an app
launched from Finder genuinely cannot see `claude`, `codex` or `gh` even though
your terminal can.

Terminal Deck handles this by asking your login shell for its `PATH` once at
startup and giving that to every session it spawns. If a CLI still is not found,
check that it is on the `PATH` your login shell exports rather than one set by an
interactive-only rc file, and look at the Setup section of the settings window,
which reports what it found.

## Verifying your own changes

If you are working on the app itself, `npm run typecheck` and `npm test` both
pass while the UI is visibly broken — that has happened, twice. The renderer can
also be mounted in a plain browser against a stubbed preload, which is the check
that has actually caught real defects:

```
npx vite --config .harness/vite.config.ts
```

It serves on port 5199.

---

# Roadmap

Source: https://terminaldeck.dev/roadmap.html

Eight phases. Seven are finished; the eighth is what stands between the current
state and something you can download and double-click.

## Done

**1 · Foundation** — Electron, React and TypeScript built with electron-vite;
process ownership with scrollback replayed across tab switches; a provider layer
that detects Claude, Codex and Gemini using the login-shell `PATH`; sidebar, tab
bar, status dots and empty state; design tokens in dark and light with
self-hosted open-licensed fonts; an atomic JSON store; a content-security policy
set from the main process.

**2 · Session intelligence** — status detection in the main process so unrendered
tabs stay accurate; a provider picker per session, project and global default;
session resume; preferences and live re-theming that recolours terminals without
a restart; desktop notifications and sounds; session titles derived from the
task; unread indicators.

**3 · Cost, context and telemetry** — transcript watcher; cost tracking per
session, project and day; token and context-window monitoring with a bloat
warning; the session inspector; deep search across past transcripts; smart
alerts.

**4 · Project workspace** — git status watcher and git panel; file tree and
viewer with syntax highlighting; quick open and command palette; GitHub
integration through `gh`; AI readiness score with one-click fixes; `.deckignore`.

**5 · Dashboard and board** — a customisable project overview on a drag-and-drop
widget grid; widgets for readiness, kanban, sessions, cost, git and GitHub; a
Kanban board per project with search and tag filtering; board and session linked,
so a card spawns or resumes a session.

**6 · Many sessions at once** — swarm mode; multiple agent profiles with
isolated logins; the full keymap and a shortcut reference sheet. Split panes were
listed here and are not done: the layout code exists but nothing renders it.

**7 · Integrations** — hooks installed into each provider's settings, namespaced
so they never collide with another tool's; MCP client and inspector; embedded
browser with element inspect; Chrome configuration import.

## Not done

**8 · Ship**

- **Code signing and notarisation.** Packaging itself is done — `npm run
  dist:mac` writes a `.dmg` and a `.zip` for arm64 and x64 — but `identity: null`
  is set deliberately, so nothing is signed and Gatekeeper needs the right-click
  step.
- **A tested Intel build.** The x64 artefact has never been launched.
- **Split panes** — layout code in the repository, rendered nowhere.
- **Auto-updates** pointed at our own releases. The library is present; nothing
  calls it yet.
- **Peer-to-peer session sharing** — read-only or read-write, with PIN auth. The
  single biggest remaining feature, and the only one that would need
  infrastructure.
- **Translations.** The app is English only.
- **Icon and brand assets.**

Linux and Windows are not on this list because they are not scheduled. The app
has only ever been run and verified on macOS.

## Known follow-ups

- The chunked transcript reader is written three times over — once each for cost,
  insights and search. All three are tested and working, so lifting them into one
  helper carries regression risk for no user-facing gain, and it waits.
- Escape-to-close on dialogs is correct in code but has never been confirmed by a
  real keypress, because synthetic key events were not delivered during testing.

## Open questions

- The name is provisional. It lives in one file, so changing it is one edit.
- Whether peer-to-peer sharing is wanted at all.

---

# Privacy

Source: https://terminaldeck.dev/privacy.html

Terminal Deck has no account, no sign-in, no telemetry and no analytics. It has
no server of its own to send anything to. Everything below is a description of
the code, not a promise about it.

## The app

### What it reads

- **Agent transcripts.** Claude Code writes JSONL transcripts under
  `~/.claude/projects/`. Terminal Deck reads them — that is where cost, context
  use, search results, session insights and chat mode all come from. It reads
  them; it does not copy or upload them.
- **Your project folder**, for the file tree, the file viewer, quick open and the
  readiness checks.
- **Git state**, by running `git`.
- **GitHub data**, by running the `gh` CLI you have already authenticated.
  Terminal Deck does not hold a GitHub token.
- **Your MCP configuration**, so the inspector lists the servers you already
  configured rather than keeping a second list.

### What it writes

- Projects, preferences and window bounds, in a `state.json` inside the app's own
  user-data directory.
- Board cards and dashboard layouts, per project.
- Hooks, into each agent CLI's real settings file — always tagged
  `terminaldeck-hook`, and never removing an entry that is not ours. The original
  file is backed up to `~/.terminaldeck/hook-backups/` first.

### What it sends

Nothing, on its own. There is no analytics SDK in the dependency list, no crash
reporter, and no update check — the auto-updater is listed as a dependency but
nothing calls it yet.

The network traffic you will see comes from things you started:

- **The agent CLIs.** Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI talk to their own
  vendors under their own terms. Terminal Deck starts them as ordinary processes
  and never sees or stores your API keys — those stay in the CLI's own
  configuration and, on macOS, in the Keychain.
- **The embedded browser**, which loads the pages you ask it to. Guest pages run
  in an isolated session and can only report facts about a clicked element back
  to the app; they cannot reach into it. Typing something that is not a URL into
  the address bar searches DuckDuckGo.
- **`git` and `gh`**, when you use the git or GitHub panels.

### Support bundles

A diagnostics bundle exists to be pasted into an issue, which makes it the single
most likely place for a credential to escape. Everything in one passes through a
redactor first: known secret literals, then structure — private-key blocks,
credentials inside URLs, `Authorization` headers, assignments whose key says the
value is a secret — then known token prefixes, then an entropy sweep for long,
dense strings that carry no other meaning. Ambiguous strings are redacted rather
than kept, on the grounds that losing information is cheap and leaking one is
not. Nothing is sent anywhere; the bundle is yours to share or not.

## This website

terminaldeck.dev is static HTML and CSS. It sets no cookies, stores nothing in
your browser, runs no analytics, and makes no requests to any other host — the
two typefaces are served from this domain, and there is no embedded video, no
comment widget, no tag manager and no font CDN. There is nothing here to consent
to, which is why you were not asked.

If the site is served from GitHub Pages or a similar host, that host will see the
ordinary request information any web server sees. That is between you and them;
it does not reach us.

## Checking any of this

All of it is verifiable rather than trusted: read the source, or watch the app's
network traffic. If a claim on this page turns out not to match the code, the
claim is the bug.
